title: The difference that decides
outcomes: Names the biggest differences between the two sides before choosing a move
Sees that king position can outweigh an extra pawn
Predicts whether a one-feature change alters the verdict, and which differences do not matter

steps.text: Before you look for moves, list the **differences between the two sides**: material, king positions, open lines, weak squares. Each difference suggests a possibility. Then ask which one decides the position. A difference does not always favour the side that seems better: here White has the extra pawn, but White also has the exposed king.

steps.caption: Black to move. White is a pawn ahead. List the differences between the two sides before you look for a move.

line.say: Rxg2+: the rook goes to g2 with check, and the queen is ready to join it on the g-file.
Check: the king is hunted and Black mates by force.

steps.text: The method is easiest when the two sides look alike, because then few differences exist to weigh. Counting material is a *rule of thumb*, and an exposed king can outweigh an extra pawn. Change one feature and the verdict can change; change a feature that plays no part and nothing changes. **Ask of each difference: what does it allow?**

steps.title: One difference changed
steps.prompt: Compare each position with the one where Rxg2+ worked. White's king stands on b1 in the second; a pawn stands on a3 in the third. Predict whether the sacrifice still wins, then check.
Before you listed the differences: which one did you look at first, material or the kings? On paper, write the three biggest differences in one of your own games.
